lesson_title: Two Maps, One Town: The Drawing and the Photograph
hook_text: Your Geography exam gives you the same town twice. One is a drawing. One is a photo. Pick the wrong one and you lose the marks.
clip_script: Every Grade 9 map question hands you two maps of the same place. Map one: the topographic map, scale 1 to 50 000. It is a drawing, seen from straight above. Blue lines for rivers, black squares for buildings, brown contour lines every 20 metres for the hills. One centimetre on it is 500 metres on the ground, so two centimetres is a kilometre. One sheet covers about 25 by 28 kilometres. Map two: the orthophoto, scale 1 to 10 000. It is a real aerial photograph, taken straight down and then corrected so the scale is the same everywhere. Contours every 5 metres. One centimetre is only 100 metres. Twenty-five orthophotos fit inside one topographic sheet. Now the trap. Which one is the larger scale? The orthophoto. Zoomed in, things look larger, you see a smaller area in more detail. Distance between towns? Use the drawing. Count the houses in a village? Use the photograph. Two maps, two jobs.
visual_style: A town seen from a hill; the view flattens into a topographic map with symbols, then a straight-down aerial photo slides beside it; a small block on the map lights up and zooms into the photo; a five-by-five grid of photos fills the map sheet.
mood: Confident, clear, a little playful on the trap.
pacing: Fast hook, steady on the two scales, a pause on the trap question, quick close on the two jobs.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to read a sheet reference, convert both scales and spot features on an orthophoto.
